summary:
Morocco criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 489 of the penal code, which punishes "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex with six months to three years of imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is applied with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. Human Rights Watch recorded Article 489 in its April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" among the statutes used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the wider region.

Trans visitors face a further layer of exposure that the statute does not name. Cairo 52's country review finds no specific legal provisions governing transition, yet documents de facto criminalisation under Article 498, where morality charges follow gender-expression discrepancies and arrest produces involuntary outing. The Cairo 52 report "A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco" (January 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla), drawn from interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, describes an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility and finds that Article 489 is weaponised to arrest trans people on the basis of gender expression alone.

No legal gender recognition pathway exists for trans people. A recognition process introduced in 2021 is open to intersex people only. Gender-affirming healthcare operates without any regulatory framework, a gap that pushes some residents into self-medication, and the Grand Mufti opposes transition. Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreign patients while enforcing what the 2026 report characterises as a de facto prohibition on the same care for its own citizens.

Two documented cases show how gender expression is policed in practice. In November 2024 Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh on suspicion of being transgender and alleges that police forced her to display her genitals; she spent about a month in jail. In January 2019 El País reported that after a minor traffic accident in Marrakesh, a cross-dressing man identified as Chafiq was handcuffed, filmed by bystanders and by police officers, and had his identity documents photographed and posted online. He subsequently sought asylum in Europe.

Public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment, and the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations. Human Rights Watch documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment directed at presumed gay and bisexual men. Police retain wide discretion throughout the country, and the documented incidents occurred in a major tourist centre rather than in any marginalised quarter.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between Morocco's medical reputation and its current domestic position is stark. The country hosted pioneering gender-affirming surgery for foreign patients, yet residents are now denied that care under an unwritten prohibition, so a visitor's nationality may shape access in ways the law does not state.

Regional legal patterns shape enforcement. The Human Rights Watch annex covering laws used against same-sex conduct and gender expression places Morocco within a broader statutory cluster, and the 170 charges recorded in 2018 indicate sustained use of the penal code rather than isolated prosecutions.

The UN Human Rights Council adopted the sexual orientation and gender identity resolution in September 2014, establishing an international scrutiny framework that formally applies to Morocco. Whether that scrutiny has altered policing practice is not evidenced in the sources.

The 2019 humiliation case ended in a claim for asylum in Europe, an outcome that indicates the perceived absence of domestic remedy for a person targeted over gender expression.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition; the 2021 recognition process covers intersex people only, and the Grand Mufti has publicly opposed transition.

The absence of any gender-affirming healthcare framework leaves residents to source hormones and related care without clinical supervision, and Cairo 52 records self-medication as a consequence.

Cairo 52's country review describes de facto criminalisation under Article 498 for residents, where morality charges arise from gender-expression discrepancies and arrest entails involuntary outing.

Human Rights Watch documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment targeting presumed gay and bisexual men, and Outright International reports that the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations, narrowing organised recourse.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 489 has been charged against foreign visitors on gender-expression grounds, as distinct from the two documented police incidents, is not resolved in the available sources.

The current operation and eligibility scope of the 2021 intersex recognition process is stated only in the Cairo 52 review and has not been independently verified here.

Practical effect of the 2014 UN Human Rights Council resolution on Moroccan enforcement is not sourced; its existence as a scrutiny framework is the only established point.

The ILGA "State-Sponsored Homophobia" survey of May 2008 predates the documented cases and its figures have not been checked against current statute, so it is treated as background rather than current law.

Differences in policing between tourist centres and other cities are not established by the sources; both documented incidents occurred in Marrakesh, which is a single data point rather than a measured pattern.
